pageTitle: Morse: The Decentralized Headless CMS Protocol
heading: What is Morse?
text: Morse lets developers build content applications (blogs, knowledge bases, gated media platforms) where the backend is an open protocol instead of a vendor service. You define content structures, set access policies, and publish through a CLI or TypeScript SDK; the contracts handle identity, permissions, and revision history so there is no central point of failure to trust or migrate away from.

pageTitle: Morse: The Decentralized Headless CMS Protocol
heading: Why Morse?
text: Traditional headless CMSs create several long-term constraints: Trust concentration: one vendor backend controls all identity and data Weak portability: publication identity and permissions do not travel with you Opaque history: change and authorization history is hidden inside a closed system Vendor lock-in: migrating requires re-building your backend from scratch Morse solves these while keeping the ergonomics of headless CMS architecture. Publication identity is canonical on-chain. Write permissions are capability-based and verifiable. Every revision is auditable. And any team can integrate

heading: Core Concepts
text: Understand the fundamental building blocks of the Morse protocol: the data model, authorization system, storage strategy, and how on-chain and off-chain components interact.

heading: The data model
text: Morse organizes content in a four-level hierarchy. Each level is stored on-chain and has a clear responsibility: Level 1 Publication → e.g. my-blog, a brand-level content domain Level 2 Collection → e.g. articles, site-pages (content lanes) Level 3 Entry → e.g. welcome-post, a single content unit Level 4 Revision → immutable snapshot: blob reference + metadata

heading: A concrete example
text: Imagine you run a team blog. Here is how it maps to the Morse data model: Publication team-blog: your brand-level content domain, registered with a unique slug Collection articles: one content lane for blog posts (blob mode, since each post is independent) Entry #0 welcome-post: your first blog post, assigned the monotonic ID 0 Revision 0: the initial published version. public_head points here, so readers see it immediately Revision 1: an updated draft. draft_head points here, but public_head still points to revision 0; readers see the original until you explicitly promote the draft Editors op

heading: Publications
text: Think of a publication as your project or site. It is the top-level namespace that groups all your content together. Every publication gets a unique slug (like my-blog) that acts as a human-readable identifier across the protocol. All collections, entries, and permissions live under this single umbrella. See Publications for the full reference →

heading: Collections
text: Collections are how you organize entries within a publication, similar to folders or content types. For example, a blog might have an articles collection and a site-pages collection. When you create a collection, you choose how its content is stored: individually as separate blobs (good for standalone posts or images) or as a shared document that can be patched in place (good for structured data like settings or configuration). See Collections for the full reference →

heading: Entries & revisions
text: Entries are the actual content pieces: a blog post, an image, a page. Every edit creates a new revision rather than overwriting the previous one, giving you a complete version history whose on-chain record is immutable. The system tracks two pointers for each entry: a draft head for work-in-progress and a public head that readers see. This lets drafts evolve privately while production clients serve stable published content. See Entries for the full reference →

heading: How publishing works
text: End-to-end flow when you publish content: Authenticate: hold a PublisherCap for the target publication Upload: upload content bytes to Walrus, get a blob reference Register: create an entry on-chain storing the blob reference, content type, and access policy Heads update: public_head and/or draft_head update based on encryption status Read: any client resolves the entry and fetches the payload from Walrus

heading: Capability-based authorization
text: Instead of usernames and passwords, Morse uses on-chain capability objects to manage permissions. Owning the right object in your wallet proves you have permission to act. No login server required. Morse separates ownership from publishing using two types of capability tokens. An OwnerCap (one per publication) controls administrative operations like issuing permissions and deleting the publication. PublisherCaps (many per publication) grant write access and are bound to a specific holder address. Revocation uses a denylist-based model: issuing caps is cheap (zero table writes), and only revoca

heading: Walrus storage
text: The Sui blockchain only stores references (pointers) to your content, not the content bytes themselves. The actual payloads live on Walrus, a decentralized storage network designed for large data. This separation keeps on-chain costs low while keeping your content verifiable: payloads stay available for the storage period you fund (measured in Walrus epochs) and can be renewed at any time. Walrus is format-agnostic, so Morse can support JSON, Markdown, images, video, or any custom schema. See Collections → Storage modes for storage mode details →

heading: Access control
text: Morse can gate content behind on-chain encryption using Seal. Only users who meet specific on-chain conditions can decrypt and read the content. This means access rules are enforced by the blockchain itself, not by a server you have to trust. This approach enables paid subscriptions, token-gated access, team-only content, and other models, all without a centralized gatekeeper. See Access Control for the full reference →

heading: Off-chain services
text: The blockchain is the canonical source of truth, but off-chain services improve the developer experience. Morse provides optional infrastructure like an indexer (for fast search and queries) and a content API (for read access) so you do not have to query the chain directly. These services make building apps on Morse faster and simpler, but they are not required. pageTitle: Fix a typo without losing history
heading: Why revisions, not edits
text: Morse never overwrites a post. Every change is a new revision appended to the entry, and every earlier revision stays readable forever. An entry keeps two pointers, the public head (what readers get) and the draft head (what you are working on). Fixing a typo moves the public head, it does not erase anything. text entry 0 revision 0 public "Hello from Morse" <- still readable revision 1 public "Hello from Morse" (fixed) <- public head Everything below assumes you have the publication and collection from Launch a blog set as your active context. heading: Import an existing Markdown site

heading: What this does
text: You have a folder of Markdown posts from Hugo, Astro, Jekyll, Obsidian or a plain repo. This recipe publishes each file as one Morse entry, writes a small map from filename to entry id, and lets you run it again later without duplicating anything. Morse stores bytes as they are, so front matter goes in untouched and your existing renderer keeps working.

heading: Lay out the folder

heading: Dry run
text: Count the files and estimate storage before spending WAL. Walrus charges per blob per epoch, so the total size and the epoch count are what matter. bash Copy $ ls content/posts/*.md | wc -l $ du -ch content/posts/*.md | tail -1

heading: Publish everything
text: The script publishes every file that is not yet in the map. The entry name is the filename without the extension. --json gives machine-readable output, -q hides the progress lines, and jq pulls the entry id out. bashimport.sh Copy #!/usr/bin/env bash set -euo pipefail MAP=morse-map.json EPOCHS=${EPOCHS:-30} [ -f "$MAP" ] || echo '{}' > "$MAP" for f in content/posts/*.md; do name=$(basename "$f" .md) if jq -e --arg n "$name" '.[$n]' "$MAP" >/dev/null; then echo "skip $name (already published)"; continue fi echo "add $name" out=$(morse --json -q entry add "$name" --file "$f" --epochs "$EPOCHS")

heading: Keep the map
text: Commit morse-map.json next to your content. It is the only thing that ties a filename to an entry id, and your site generator or reader app needs it to fetch bodies from Walrus. jsonmorse-map.json { "2026-09-01-why-a-protocol": { "entryId": 0, "file": "2026-09-01-why-a-protocol" }, "2026-09-14-dual-head-revisions": { "entryId": 1, "file": "2026-09-14-dual-head-revisions" } }

heading: Re-running safely
text: New files get added, existing ones are skipped. To push an edited post as a new revision rather than a new entry, look the id up in the map and use revision publish-direct: bash Copy $ id=$(jq -r '.["2026-09-14-dual-head-revisions"].entryId' morse-map.json) $ morse revision publish-direct "$id" --file content/posts/2026-09-14-dual-head-revisions.md --epochs 30 A simple way to automate that: store each file's content hash in the map and publish a revision whenever the hash changes. Left as a ten-line exercise, or ask your agent, see Let an AI agent publish.

heading: How write access works
text: There are no user accounts in Morse. Write access is an object. When you created your publication you received an OwnerCap (full control) and a PublisherCap (can add entries and revisions). To let someone else publish, the owner mints a new PublisherCap bound to their address. To take it away, the owner revokes it. The co-author never needs your key, and you never need theirs. CapabilityWho holds itCan doOwnerCapYou, one per publicationIssue and revoke publisher caps, transfer ownership, deletePublisherCapYou and anyone you issue one toCreate collections, add entries, append and publish revisi

heading: Owner: issue a cap
text: You need the co-author's Sui address. From your machine, with the publication active: bash Copy $ morse status # confirm the active publication $ morse cap issue 0xCOAUTHOR_ADDRESS output Resolving OwnerCap... Issued PublisherCap 0x3f8a...c21e to 0xCOAUTHOR_ADDRESS. (tx: 4Hn9xT...q2Wd) network: testnet Save the cap id, you will need it to revoke. The cap is sent to the co-author's address as part of the same transaction, there is nothing for you to hand over.

heading: Co-author: set up and publish
text: On the co-author's machine, same setup as Launch a blog, then point at your publication by slug: bash Copy $ npm i -g @arcadiasystems/morse-cli $ morse config add testnet --network testnet $ morse account import $ morse cap list # the new cap shows up here $ morse use my-blog-1760000000 posts $ morse entry add guest-post --file guest-post.md --epochs 14 The CLI finds the right PublisherCap automatically from the active account. If the co-author holds caps for several publications, --publisher-cap <id> picks one explicitly. Reads by slug need an account, reads by id do not morse use <slug> reso

heading: Owner: see who can write
text: bash Copy $ morse cap list 0xCOAUTHOR_ADDRESS There is no team page, and anyone can run this query on chain. It lists every PublisherCap the address holds, revoked ones included, with no revoked marker: a cap in the list is not proof that it still works. To know for sure, keep the cap ids you issue and revoke, or watch for the publication's PublisherCapIssued and PublisherCapRevoked events.

heading: Revoke, and what the co-author sees
text: bash Copy $ morse cap revoke 0x3f8a...c21e The CLI asks you to confirm before it revokes. In a script, put the global --yes before the subcommand: morse --yes cap revoke 0x3f8a...c21e. Without it a non-interactive shell refuses with exit 2. From the next transaction on, every write the co-author attempts with that cap aborts on chain. revision publish-from-draft, for example, exits with code 4 and says the cap has been revoked. entry add and entry add-encrypted are the exception: they upload to Walrus first, so the upload is paid for, and then exit with code 1 and an "uploaded but the on-chain

heading: Rotate instead of transfer
text: Do not transfer caps between people A cap's holder is fixed when it is issued. cap transfer moves the object but not the binding, so the recipient cannot use it and the original holder cannot either. To hand write access to a new person: owner revokes the old cap, owner issues a new one. bash Copy $ morse cap revoke 0xOLD_CAP_ID $ morse cap issue 0xNEW_PERSON_ADDRESS Transferring the whole publication is different and final: morse publication transfer-ownership 0xNEW_OWNER hands over the OwnerCap with no undo. Existing publisher caps keep working until the new owner revokes them.

heading: What encryption gives you today
text: Morse encrypts content client side with Seal before it goes to Walrus. The decryption rule is a Move function on Sui: a Seal key server only releases its share if the caller holds an active PublisherCap for that publication. So today, encrypted means readable by your team: everyone with write access, nobody else, and no server of yours in the middle. The entry was created as a draft. Encrypted entries always start as drafts, because publishing is a separate decision. Collecti

pageTitle: Encrypt a post for your team
heading: Read it as a cap holder
text: Reading is entry decrypt, not entry read. The CLI signs a short-lived session key with your account, asks the key servers for shares, and decrypts locally. bash Copy $ morse entry decrypt 5 --via-aggregator --out q4-plan.recovered.md $ diff q4-plan.md q4-plan.recovered.md && echo identical Anyone you issued a cap to in Add a co-author can run the same command from their own wallet. pageTitle: Encrypt a post for your team
heading: Release it to everyone
text: A draft is visible as an entry on chain but is not the public head, and for encrypted content it stays that way: published revisions are always public and unencrypted, so the team keeps reading the draft with entry decrypt. The CLI will not add a public revision to an encrypted entry. Both of these exit with code 2 and "Encrypted revisions are not yet supported": bash Copy $ morse revision publish-from-draft 5 0 --file q4-plan.md # refused $ morse revision publish-direct 5 --file q4-plan.md # refused To release the text, publish the plaintext as a new, ordinary entry with morse entry add q4-pl

pageTitle: Encrypt a post for your team
heading: Rotate a key, revoke a reader
text: Access is enforced at decryption time, every time. Revoking a cap cuts off a reader even for content they could read yesterday: bash Copy $ morse cap revoke 0xTHEIR_CAP_ID Note what this does and does not do. It stops the key servers from serving that wallet from now on. It does not un-read anything they already decrypted and saved. Same as any system, but worth saying out loud to a team.

pageTitle: Encrypt a post for your team
heading: Honest limits
text: QuestionAnswer todayCan I sell access to a post?Not yet. The subscription policy exists on chain but its approval function is not built. It is on the roadmap.Can a reader get read access without write access?Not with Seal gating. A PublisherCap is both. Keep the team small.Who runs the key servers?Seal key servers on testnet, two of three shares needed by default. If they are down, nobody can decrypt, including you.Is the ciphertext safe on Walrus?Walrus stores the bytes anyone can fetch. The key never leaves the key servers and your client.

heading: Publications
text: A publication is the top-level permission management and identity boundary for a content domain in Morse. Everything (collections, entries, permissions) lives inside a publication.

heading: What is a publication?
text: A Publication is a shared Sui object that acts as the root container for one content brand or site. It bundles: A human-readable name (display label) An immutable, globally unique slug (canonical URL key) A collection map holding all named content lanes A revocation denylist for publisher capabilities Move public struct Publication has key { id: UID, name: String, slug: String, collections: VecMap<String, Collection>, revoked_publisher_caps: Table<ID, bool>, } The Publication type has key ability but no store. Sharing and transfer are gated through this module's own functions, enforced by the

heading: The slug system
text: Every publication is identified by a slug: a short, lowercase string that becomes its canonical identifier across the protocol. Slugs are enforced to be globally unique by the PublicationRegistry.

heading: Slug rules
text: RuleConstraint CharactersLowercase letters a-z, digits 0-9, hyphens - Length1 to 64 characters Edge hyphensCannot start or end with - UniquenessMust be globally unique while the publication is active ImmutabilityCannot be changed after publication creation Examples // valid slugs "my-blog" "acme-corp" "docs2025" // invalid slugs "-leading-hyphen" // ESlugInvalidEdgeHyphen "trailing-hyphen-" // ESlugInvalidEdgeHyphen "UPPERCASE" // ESlugInvalidChar "spaces not allowed" // ESlugInvalidChar "" // ESlugEmpty

heading: Collections
text: A collection is a named content lane inside a publication. It groups related entries together and determines how their Walrus payload references are stored.

heading: What is a collection?
text: Collections organize entries into predictable buckets for editorial workflows and API consumers. A publication holds collections in a VecMap<String, Collection> keyed by name. The choice of VecMap reflects the expectation that a publication will have only a small number of named collections. heading: Storage modes
text: Every collection has a storage_mode set at creation that controls how entry revisions reference Walrus content. mode 0 Blob Mode Each entry revision references a standalone Walrus Blob object by its Sui object ID. mode 1 Quilt Mode Each entry revision stores a 37-byte QuiltPatchId pointing to a patch within a shared Walrus Quilt blob.

heading: Blob mode
text: In blob mode, every revision stores a BlobRef::Blob(ID), the Sui object ID of a standalone Walrus Blob. Each entry revision is fully independent: uploading new content creates a new blob, and the old blobs remain accessible by their IDs. Best for: Articles, blog posts, documentation pages Media libraries (images, videos, audio) Any collection where entries change independently and frequently Situations where you want maximum operational simplicity

heading: Quilt mode

heading: Entries & Revisions
text: An entry is a single content unit within a collection. Revisions are its immutable history. The dual-head model lets drafts evolve freely while production readers always see a stable published state.

heading: The dual-head model

heading: Walrus blob requirements

heading: Blob lifecycle: epochs, expiry, renewal

heading: Access Control

heading: Recipient Files
text: Recipient files are Morse's second content model: standalone files on Walrus with a per-file recipient list enforced on-chain. Encrypt a file for specific addresses, share it with a single string, and revoke access at decrypt time. No publication required.

Each file is an independent shared object on Sui (RecipientFile, defined in the recipient_file Move module) that references a Walrus blob and embeds its own recipient set. There is no shared ACL across files and no capability objects involved. heading: CLI Overview
text: morse-cli is the command-line client for the Morse decentralized CMS. It signs with a locally encrypted key, stores content on Walrus, and encrypts private entries with Seal: the same protocol surface as the SDK, driven from your terminal. Runs on Node or Bun and targets testnet or Walrus Mainnet. Published on npm · testnet and mainnet Install @arcadiasystems/morse-cli from npm. It targets testnet unless you choose mainnet with --network, MORSE_NETWORK or a profile. The contracts are unaudited and mainnet spends real SUI and WAL, so test on testnet first.

heading: Installing
text: The published binary is a Node-targeted bundle. You need Node (≥ 18) or Bun (≥ 1.2) to run it. bash Copy npm i -g @arcadiasystems/morse-cli morse --help Also available via bun add -g or pnpm add -g. Or run without installing: bash Copy npx @arcadiasystems/morse-cli --help

heading: Security model
text: Private keys are stored in an encrypted keystore (scrypt + AES-256-GCM) and unlocked by a password. Keys are never accepted as command-line flags. They come only from an interactive hidden prompt, the MORSE_PRIVATE_KEY env var, or the encrypted keystore. Keystore files are written chmod 600; group- or world-readable key files are refused on read. Keys are never printed or logged, including under --debug. The sole exception is account export, which deliberately reveals a key: interactive-only, requires confirmation, unavailable in --json. For CI, set MORSE_PRIVATE_KEY (raw key, never persisted)

heading: Publishing a new revision
text: Append a new public revision directly, or stage a draft first and promote it. Revisions are append-only; existing revisions are never edited in place. Two heads track progress: draftHead (work in progress) and publicHead (the live version).

heading: Option A: publish direct
text: Skip the draft stage and append a new public revision in one step. This updates publicHead immediately. bash Copy echo "hello morse, edited" > post.md morse revision publish-direct 0 --file post.md

heading: Option B: draft then publish
text: Stage a draft revision first (updates draftHead only), then promote it to a public revision. By default, publish-from-draft reuses the draft's content; pass --file to replace it with new content. Useful when you want to review before going live. bash Copy echo "hello morse, draft" > draft.md morse revision append-draft 0 --file draft.md morse revision publish-from-draft 0 1 See also: SDK Cookbooks → Publishing a new revision

heading: Encrypted content
text: Morse uses Seal for on-chain access control over encrypted content. When you add an encrypted entry, the CLI handles Seal key negotiation automatically. bash Copy echo "members only" > secret.txt morse entry add-encrypted members --file secret.txt morse entry decrypt 1 --via-aggregator --out recovered.txt Encrypted entries are always drafts Encrypted entries are always created as drafts. You must explicitly publish them with a separate transaction after adding. Retrieve encrypted content with entry decrypt plus a PublisherCap, not entry read. heading: Delegating write access
text: Morse separates ownership (OwnerCap) from publishing (PublisherCap). The owner issues a cap bound to a co-author's address, granting them write access. Once issued, the co-author can publish entries using their own key. Revoking the cap causes further writes to abort on-chain. See Access Control → Issuing publisher caps for details. As the owner, issue a cap to grant write access and revoke it to remove access: bash Copy morse cap issue 0xCO_AUTHOR_ADDRESS morse cap revoke 0xCAP_ID As a cap holder, list your caps or permanently destroy a specific cap: bash Copy morse cap list morse cap destroy

heading: Transferring ownership
text: The owner can transfer the publication's OwnerCap to another address, handing over full governance: the recipient becomes the new owner and can issue, revoke, and manage caps. bash Copy morse publication transfer-ownership 0xNEW_OWNER One-way for the sender Once transferred, the original owner loses all governance rights immediately. The new owner could transfer back, but there is no built-in undo. See also: SDK Cookbooks → Transferring ownership

heading: Deleting and tearing down
text: Deletion is bottom-up: remove entries first, then collections, then the publication. Each container must be empty before it can be deleted. Entry IDs are permanently retired on deletion and never reused. See Entries → Deleting an entry for details. bash Copy morse entry delete 0 morse entry delete 1 morse collection delete posts morse publication delete See also: SDK Cookbooks → Deleting and tearing down

heading: Scripting and CI
text: Authenticate with env vars (no prompts), skip confirmations with --yes, and parse --json on stdout. heading: Transferring ownership
text: Transfer the OwnerCap to a new address. The recipient gains governance rights: issuing/revoking publisher caps and deleting the publication. heading: Encrypted files and Seal on Walrus Mainnet
text: An encrypted upload encrypts the file under Seal before it leaves the browser, then creates the file and binds its Seal identity in one transaction. The connected wallet is always a recipient, so the owner can always decrypt. At decrypt time, Seal key servers check the file's recipient set on-chain, and a wallet outside it gets no key. Decrypting takes one wallet popup to create a Seal SessionKey, which is reused across files until it expires (10 minutes by default; set it with ttlMin). Testnet pins an open set of key servers, so encryption works there with no setup. Walrus Mainnet pins none,

heading: Limitations
text: Storage is a lease. Walrus stores a file for at most 53 epochs ahead, then it expires. An epoch is about 1 day on testnet and about 2 weeks on Walrus Mainnet. No file listing yet. A RecipientFile is a shared object, so it never shows up in a wallet's owned objects. Listing a wallet's files needs an event indexer, and the package ships no listing UI until one exists. Recipients are set at upload. The components do not change recipients afterwards. The SDK's owner-only addRecipient and removeRecipient do.

heading: Contract Overview

Testnet deployment Use SDK Setup → morseConfig() to get the current package ID, original ID, and registry ID. These values update automatically when the contract is upgraded.

heading: What PTBs give you
text: Full transaction control Compose multiple Move calls in a single PTB: create a publication, add a collection, and publish an entry atomically. No SDK abstraction layer Call the contract functions directly. Useful when the SDK does not expose a wrapper for your use case or when you need fine-grained control. Custom batching Delete 50 entries, 3 collections, and a publication in one transaction. The SDK processes these sequentially; PTBs batch them. BCS encoding Pass Option<vector<u8>> and other Move types directly via @mysten/sui/bcs. Required for encrypted entries and quilt patches.

heading: Known limitations
text: No encrypted publish path. publish_from_draft and publish_direct hardcode encrypted = false. Encrypted content stays as drafts. See Entries → Adding an entry for the full lifecycle. Only the Publisher access policy is enforced. The Subscription policy constant is defined but the approval entry point is not yet implemented. All blobs must be deletable. The contract calls blob.is_deletable() and aborts if a permanent blob is passed. Single entry point module. All public functions live in publication::publication. The other modules are internal.

heading: Adding an entry
text: Upload content to Walrus first, then pass the resulting Blob object ID to add_entry_to_collection. The blob argument is a reference to a Walrus Blob Sui object (&Blob), not a blob ID hash. Only deletable blobs are accepted. heading: Delegating write access
text: The owner issues PublisherCap objects to grant write access to co-authors. Revocation adds the cap ID to an on-chain denylist; all subsequent writes using that cap abort with EPublisherCapRevoked. See Access Control for the full capability model.

heading: Issuing a PublisherCap
text: Only the OwnerCap holder can issue new caps. heading: Deleting and tearing down
text: Deletion is strictly bottom-up. The Move layer enforces this: delete_collection calls table::destroy_empty on the entries table and aborts if any entries remain. delete_publication calls collections.destroy_empty() and aborts if any collections remain. Entry IDs are permanently retired on deletion and never reused.

heading: Troubleshooting
text: Move aborts surface as MoveAbort errors in the RPC response with a module name and numeric code. The table below maps the most common codes to their cause. CodeErrorModuleCause 6 ESlugAlreadyExists publication A publication with that slug already exists in the registry. 2 EUnauthorized publication The cap's publication_id does not match the publication object passed in the call. 4 EPublisherCapWrongHolder publication The transaction sender does not match cap.holder. 5 EPublisherCapRevoked publication The cap ID is on the publication's revoked denylist. heading: Glossary
text: Terms used throughout the Morse protocol and this documentation.

heading: A
text: Access Policy A numeric constant stored per revision that defines who can read the payload. Current values: 0 (public), 1 (publisher), 2 (subscription, reserved). Strictly coupled with the encrypted flag: public (0) requires encrypted=false; publisher (1) requires encrypted=true.

heading: B
text: Blob Mode Storage mode 0 for collections. Each entry revision stores a BlobRef::Blob(ID) pointing to an independent Walrus Blob object by Sui object ID. Best for growing, frequently-changing collections. BlobRef A Move enum stored per revision that abstracts the two Walrus payload reference formats. Variants: Blob(ID) for standalone blobs, QuiltPatch(vector<u8>) for 37-byte quilt patch identifiers.

heading: C
text: Capability A Move object that proves authorization to perform a specific action. Morse has two capability types: OwnerCap (admin authority) and PublisherCap (write authority). Capabilities cannot be fabricated; they can only be issued by the protocol. CMS Content Management System. Software for creating, organizing, and publishing structured digital content. Morse implements a decentralized, headless CMS protocol where permission management lives on-chain rather than in a centralized backend. Collection A named content lane inside a publication. Holds entries in a table keyed by monotonic entr

heading: D
text: dCMS Decentralized Content Management System, the category Morse belongs to. Publication identity, authorization, and state transitions are governed on-chain; payloads are stored off-chain in decentralized storage (Walrus). Denylist The revocation model used for PublisherCaps. A Table<ID, bool> on each publication stores IDs of revoked caps. Issuance writes nothing to the table; only revocations write. This optimizes for the common case where revocations never occur. Draft Head An Option<u64> pointer in an Entry that tracks the index of the latest draft revision. May be None if no draft has be

heading: E
text: Entry A single content unit within a collection. Holds a name, an immutable revision vector, and two head pointers. Identified by a stable monotonic entry_id within its collection. Entry ID A u64 assigned to an entry when added to a collection. Values start at 0 and increment monotonically. IDs are never reused after deletion (stable for external references). EntryRevision The Move struct that stores a single revision's data: blob_ref, content_type, encrypted, access_policy, seal_id, and author. Has store, drop abilities. Stored in an entry's revisions vector. Epoch A Walrus storage duration u

heading: G
text: gRPC A high-performance RPC framework used by SuiGrpcClient from @mysten/sui/grpc. The Morse SDK requires gRPC transport for all Sui interactions. Works in modern browsers without a proxy. See SDK Overview → Known limitations for JSON-RPC fallback status.

heading: H
text: Headless CMS A CMS architecture that separates content management from presentation. The CMS manages content and metadata; client applications decide how to render it. Content is delivered through APIs. Morse follows this model while decentralizing identity, authorization, and state transitions. Holder The address field on a PublisherCap that binds the capability to a specific wallet. Write operations check that tx.sender() == cap.holder. A cap cannot be shared between addresses.

heading: I
text: Indexer The off-chain service that listens to on-chain events and builds a read-optimized index of publications, collections, and entries. Currently planned. See How Morse Works → Off-chain services.

heading: M
text: Monotonic ID A collection-scoped, auto-incrementing integer assigned to each entry. IDs are never reused after deletion. See Entries → Entry IDs. Move The programming language used for smart contracts on the Sui blockchain. Morse's on-chain logic is written in Move.

heading: O
text: OwnerCap The admin capability for a publication. Exactly one exists per publication. Grants authority to issue and revoke publisher caps, delete the publication, and transfer ownership. Has key ability only. Transferable via transfer_owner_cap.

heading: P
text: Publication The top-level Morse content domain. A shared Sui object that bundles a name, an immutable slug, named collections, and a revocation denylist. Created via new_publication. PublicationRegistry A shared singleton Sui object created at package deploy time. Maintains a Table<String, ID> that maps slugs to publication IDs, enforcing global slug uniqueness. Required argument for new_publication and delete_publication. Public Head An Option<u64> pointer in an Entry that tracks the index of the currently published revision. What reader-facing clients should read. Updated by publish_collecti

heading: Q
text: Quilt Mode Storage mode 1 for collections. Each entry revision stores a 37-byte QuiltPatchId pointing to a patch within a shared Walrus Quilt blob. Best for stable, grouped content sets. QuiltPatchId A 37-byte identifier used in quilt mode collections. Layout: quilt_blob_id (32 bytes) || version (1 byte) || start_index (2 bytes) || end_index (2 bytes). Stored as a BlobRef::QuiltPatch(vector<u8>).

heading: R
text: Revision An immutable version of an entry at a point in time. Stored in the entry's revisions: vector<EntryRevision>. Each revision records a BlobRef, content type, encryption state, access policy, optional Seal identity, and author address. Revisions are never mutated; edits append new ones. Revision ID The index of a revision within an entry's revisions vector. Starts at 0. Returned by all revision-appending functions. Used to reference a specific revision in publish_collection_entry_from_draft. Revocation The act of adding a PublisherCap's object ID to a publication's denylist via revoke_pu

heading: S
text: Seal Mysten Labs' on-chain access control layer for Walrus blob decryption. Morse integrates via the seal_approve_publisher entry function, which validates that an active publisher cap holder is authorized within a specific publication namespace. Seal Identity A byte vector (vector<u8>) that Seal presents to the approval function during decryption. In Morse, the format is: [publication_id (32 bytes)][policy_tag (1 byte)][nonce (variable)]. Scopes decryption approval to a specific publication and policy. Shared Object A Sui object accessible to any transaction, not owned by a single address. In

heading: T
text: Table A Sui framework type (sui::table::Table) used by Morse for dynamic key-value storage within on-chain objects. For example, collections store entries in a Table<u64, Entry>.

heading: W
text: WAL The utility token of the Walrus decentralized storage network. WAL is used to pay for blob storage and is separate from SUI (the gas token for Sui transactions). Walrus MystenLabs' decentralized blob storage network integrated with Sui. Morse stores all content payloads in Walrus; the contracts hold references (BlobRef), not the raw bytes. Walrus is format-agnostic; payload interpretation is the client's responsibility. Walrus Blob A Sui object (walrus::blob::Blob) representing a payload stored in the Walrus network. heading: Use Morse with AI
text: Morse publishes its documentation in machine-readable formats and ships agent-operable tooling, so AI coding agents can learn the protocol from current context, and then run the entire backend themselves.

heading: Machine-readable docs
text: Every page on this site is available in three agent-friendly forms. No scraping, no HTML parsing, just Markdown. Format URL Use it for llms.txt /llms.txt Compact index of all pages with one-line descriptions. Point an agent here first so it can pick which pages to read. llms-full.txt /llms-full.txt The complete documentation concatenated into a single Markdown file. One fetch gives an agent everything. Markdown twins /<page>.md Every page has a Markdown version at the same URL with .md instead of .html (e.g. /entries.md).

heading: Prime a coding agent
text: Paste one line into your agent to load the full Morse context: prompt Copy Read https://docs.morsecms.xyz/llms-full.txt, the full documentation for Morse, the decentralized headless CMS protocol on Sui + Walrus. Use it to help me build with the Morse CLI, TypeScript SDK, or Move contracts. Or fetch context on demand from a terminal-capable agent: bash Copy # Index of all pages curl -s https://docs.morsecms.xyz/llms.txt # One specific page as Markdown curl -s https://docs.morsecms.xyz/quick-start-cli.md # Everything at once curl -s https://docs.morsecms.xyz/llms-full.txt Working in a Morse proj

heading: Copy any page for AI
text: Each docs page has a Copy page button (top right of the content area) with four actions: Copy page as Markdown: puts the page's Markdown twin on your clipboard, ready to paste into any assistant. View as Markdown: opens the raw .md version in a new tab. Open in ChatGPT / Open in Claude: opens the assistant with a prompt that references this page and the full docs. There is also Ask AI in the header (or press ⌘I): type a question and it opens Claude or ChatGPT pre-loaded with the entire Morse documentation as context.

heading: Agent-first by design
text: Morse is not just documented for agents; it is operable by them. There is no dashboard signup, no API-key console, no human-only provisioning step anywhere in the protocol. Everything is a CLI command, an SDK call, or a transaction: Provision from the terminal: with morse publication create, morse collection create and morse entry add, a coding agent can go from nothing to published content without leaving the shell.
